title: Chisleu “in the twentieth year”, then Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes” — how is the year counted, and whose year is the first?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Nehemiah hears the report from Jerusalem in the month Chisleu “in the twentieth year” and speaks to the king in the month Nisan “in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes”. Elsewhere the KJV calls Chisleu the ninth month and Nisan the first. The book does not say from what point its years are counted, or whose twentieth year 1:1 means.
text: KJV Nehemiah 1:1: “The words of Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah. And it came to pass in the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as I was in Shushan the palace,” KJV Nehemiah 2:1: “And it came to pass in the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that wine was before him” KJV Zechariah 7:1: “in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu” KJV Esther 3:7: “In the first month, that is, the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus” KJV Nehemiah 5:14: “from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years” Hebrew (WLC) 1:1: וַיְהִ֤י בְחֹֽדֶשׁ־[כִּסְלֵו כ] (כִּסְלֵיו֙ ק) שְׁנַ֣ת עֶשְׂרִ֔ים [and it came to pass in the month Chislev, year twenty; the bracketed forms are the edition’s written and read spellings of the month]; 2:1: וַיְהִ֣י ׀ בְּחֹ֣דֶשׁ נִיסָ֗ן שְׁנַ֥ת עֶשְׂרִ֛ים לְאַרְתַּחְשַׁ֥סְתְּא הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ [and it came to pass in the month Nisan, year twenty of Artaxerxes the king]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:1: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν μηνὶ Χασελεῦ ἔτους εἰκοστοῦ; 2:1: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν μηνὶ Νισὰν ἔτους εἰκοστοῦ Ἀρθασασθὰ βασιλεῖ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/16/1/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/16/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZR11.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZR12.htm.
reasoning: The story runs from Chisleu to Nisan, and both are put in a twentieth year. If the year number changed with the first month, Nisan, a Chisleu of the twentieth year would be followed by a Nisan of the twenty-first; if the events are in the order told, the year did not change between them. How the years are counted decides how long Nehemiah waited and when his twelve years as governor began, and the verses quoted do not state it. Verse 1:1 also names no king.
scope: Readings that have been offered, none stated in the verses quoted: that the king’s years are counted from the day or season he began to reign, not from Nisan; that the year is counted from the autumn; that “the twentieth year” of 1:1 belongs to some other count than the king’s; or that one of the two figures has been miscopied. Hebrew and Greek have “twentieth” in both verses, as the KJV does. The month numbers are taken from Zechariah 7:1 and Esther 3:7; a whole-word search of the packaged KJV finds Chisleu only at Nehemiah 1:1 and Zechariah 7:1 and Nisan only at Nehemiah 2:1 and Esther 3:7. That is a word search, not a reading of every passage about the calendar. This is not presented as a contradiction. Brenton’s Greek prints Nehemiah as the later chapters of its Ezra pages; the address given is the page that prints this chapter. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: “The wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire” — which breaking and burning is reported to Nehemiah?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Men from Judah tell Nehemiah that the wall of Jerusalem is broken down and its gates burned. The verses do not say when or by whom this was done: whether it is the state left by the Chaldean army long before, or the result of something later.
text: KJV Nehemiah 1:2: “and I asked them concerning the Jews that had escaped, which were left of the captivity, and concerning Jerusalem” KJV Nehemiah 1:3: “And they said unto me, The remnant that are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire.” KJV Nehemiah 1:4: “when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days” KJV Nehemiah 2:3: “when the city, the place of my fathers' sepulchres, lieth waste, and the gates thereof are consumed with fire” KJV Nehemiah 2:13: “and viewed the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and the gates thereof were consumed with fire” KJV 2 Kings 25:10: “And all the army of the Chaldees, that were with the captain of the guard, brake down the walls of Jerusalem round about.” KJV Ezra 4:12: “building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations” KJV Ezra 4:23: “they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power” Hebrew (WLC) Nehemiah 1:3: וְחֹומַ֤ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֙ם֙ מְפֹרָ֔צֶת וּשְׁעָרֶ֖יהָ נִצְּת֥וּ בָאֵֽשׁ [and the wall of Jerusalem is breached and its gates have been burned with fire]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:3: καὶ τείχη Ἱερουσαλὴμ καθῃρημένα, καὶ αἱ πύλαι αὐτῆς ἐνεπρήσθησαν ἐν πυρί [and the walls of Jerusalem are pulled down, and its gates were burned with fire]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/16/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZR11.htm.
reasoning: The report sets the whole book in motion, and what it reports can be read in two ways that give different histories. 2 Kings 25:10 says the Chaldean army broke down the walls of Jerusalem round about, in the days of Nebuchadnezzar. Ezra 4 has a letter to an Artaxerxes saying the Jews “have set up the walls”, and says the king’s officers then stopped them “by force and power”. Nehemiah 1:3 names no time and no agent.
scope: Readings, none stated in the verses quoted: that the men describe the ruin left by the Chaldeans, still unrepaired; or that walls begun again in the time of Ezra 4 had since been thrown down and the gates burned, an event the verses quoted do not report. Ezra 4:12 is the wording of an accusation, not the narrator’s own statement of how far the walls had risen, and Ezra 4:23 does not say that anything was broken or burned. Nehemiah’s weeping in 1:4 is quoted for what it says; it does not show whether the news was new to him. The Greek of 1:3 has “walls” in the plural; the difference is noted and not tagged. Only the verses quoted were compared; the question of which king Artaxerxes is belongs to a published record. This is not presented as a contradiction. title: “The wood offering … as it is written in the law” — what written law is meant?
summary: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The people cast lots for “the wood offering”, to be brought by families at appointed times each year “to burn upon the altar of the Lord our God, as it is written in the law”. The two laws about wood on the altar quoted here speak of the priests laying and burning wood; they do not speak of an offering of wood brought by the people in turn.
text: KJV Nehemiah 10:34: “And we cast the lots among the priests, the Levites, and the people, for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, after the houses of our fathers, at times appointed year by year, to burn upon the altar of the Lord our God, as it is written in the law:” KJV Nehemiah 13:31: “And for the wood offering, at times appointed, and for the firstfruits” KJV Leviticus 6:12: “And the fire upon the altar shall be burning in it; it shall not be put out: and the priest shall burn wood on it every morning” KJV Leviticus 1:7: “And the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and lay the wood in order upon the fire:” Hebrew (WLC), numbered 10:35: וְהַגֹּורָלֹ֨ות הִפַּ֜לְנוּ עַל־קֻרְבַּ֣ן הָעֵצִ֗ים [and we cast the lots for the offering of the wood] … לְבַעֵ֗ר עַל־מִזְבַּח֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֔ינוּ כַּכָּת֖וּב בַּתֹּורָֽה [to burn upon the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the law]; 13:31: וּלְקֻרְבַּ֧ן הָעֵצִ֛ים בְּעִתִּ֥ים מְזֻמָּנֹ֖ות [and for the offering of the wood at appointed times]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), numbered 10:35: ἐκκαῦσαι ἑπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον Κυρίου Θεοῦ ἡμῶν, ὡς γέγραπται ἐν τῷ νόμῳ [to burn upon the altar of the Lord our God, as it is written in the law]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/16/10/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/16/13/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZR20.htm.
reasoning: The words “as it is written in the law” end the verse, and the verse does not say which of its parts they cover: the burning on the altar, or the whole arrangement of a wood offering brought by lot at set times. On the first reading the people are providing for a law about the altar fire; on the second they appeal to a written rule for the offering itself. Which is meant bears on what “the law” contained for the writer.
scope: Readings, none stated in the verses quoted: that “as it is written” refers only to burning wood on the altar, as in Leviticus 6:12; that it refers to a written rule for the wood offering that the verses quoted do not contain; or that the people’s own covenant of this chapter is counted with the law. A search of the packaged KJV for the phrase “wood offering” finds only Nehemiah 10:34 and 13:31. That is a search for a phrase: it does not show that no law elsewhere speaks of the people supplying wood, and the laws of the Pentateuch were not read through for this record. Hebrew and Greek number the verse 10:35. This is not presented as a contradiction or as an error in the passage.
